title: Protocol for a small-scale mixed methods efficacy trial of a novel co-designed digital health intervention targeting emotion dysregulation in adolescents with ADHD symptoms
description:
Introduction
Emotion dysregulation (ED) is a commonly associated feature of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adolescence, yet there is a lack of scalable interventions tailored for those with ADHD symptoms. The present article outlines the protocol for a mixed-methods single-arm small-scale efficacy trial study evaluating a novel digital health intervention (DHI) in the form of a smartphone app designed to address this gap. The intervention was co-designed with adolescents with ADHD and draws on therapeutic approaches such as psychoeducation, dialectical behaviour therapy and emotion-focused variants of cognitive behavioural therapy.
Methods and analysis
The study will use a mixed-methods pre–post design involving up to 100 participants, comprising 50 adolescents aged 11–15 years who have an ADHD diagnosis or are on a waitlist for assessment and moderate-to-severe ED, and up to 50 parents/caregivers participating as optional informants. Young people will use the intervention over a four-week period. Quantitative outcomes, including ED, adaptive ER strategy use, anxiety, and depression, will be assessed at baseline and follow-up using self-report and optional parent-report measures. Quantitative engagement data will additionally be passively collected through the DHI software. Qualitative interviews will be conducted to obtain complementary, in-depth data on user experience, perceived engagement, and the feasibility of the DHI use. Quantitative data will be analysed using linear mixed-effects regression models, and qualitative data will be analysed using thematic analysis.
Ethics and dissemination
The study received multi-tiered ethical approval by the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences, as well as the School of Philosophy, Psychology and Language Science at the University of Edinburgh. title: Emotional Mirror: A Local Multimodal Generative Framework for Synthetic Memory Reconstruction
description: This research introduces a novel human–AI collaborative framework that establishes the technical foundation for future physiologically informed design in Narrative Exposure Therapy (NET) for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). While traditional AI applications treat data as static storage, we explore how machine-learning architectures can facilitate the reconstruction and externalization of fragmented traumatic memories. The proposed framework couples a written narrative, an identity-conditioned webcam image of the human subject, and an optional physical object with a locally deployed diffusion-based generative pipeline, producing visual reconstructions under clinician-adjustable conditioning parameters. The architecture is designed for future integration with real-time autonomic signal processing, enabling physiological markers of arousal to dynamically modulate image generation during graded exposure. In the present work, we establish the underlying multimodal generative and safety infrastructure and evaluate its technical feasibility using healthy volunteers on consumer-grade hardware; no claims regarding clinical efficacy are made. Rather than attempting factual reconstruction, the framework produces an "emotional mirror" that emphasizes subjective emotional experience over objective accuracy. We conclude by discussing the ethical, technical, and translational considerations required for future clinician-supervised deployment and clinical validation.

title: Assessing Sensitivity in Youth as a Moderator of Psychopathological Outcomes Across Contexts
description: Youth differ in how strongly they respond to environmental influences, with some individuals demonstrating greater sensitivity to both adverse and supportive contexts. Environmental sensitivity (ES) has emerged as a unifying framework encompassing theories such as differential susceptibility, biological sensitivity to context, and vantage sensitivity. This scoping review examined sensitivity as a moderator of the relationship between environmental exposures and mental health outcomes in children and adolescents. The review aimed to (1) identify key markers used to approximate individual differences in sensitivity and (2) examine the methods used to measure these markers across studies. A total of 34 articles representing 37 studies were included. Markers of ES fell into five categories: phenotypic (e.g., temperament, sensitivity), genetic (e.g., 5HTTLPR, DRD4), physiological (e.g., cortisol, vagal tone), biological (e.g., prematurity), and neurobiological (e.g., amygdala activation). Phenotypic markers were most commonly studied, primarily assessed through parent- or youth-report questionnaires. Sensitivity was found to moderate the effects of various environments on mental health, with differential susceptibility emerging as the most consistently supported theoretical model. Assessment approaches varied widely in measurement tools, informants, and analytic methods depending on the marker used. Few studies used multi-informant or longitudinal methods. This review highlights the value of identifying sensitive youth who may be more responsive to both risk and protective factors and highlights the need for more methodologically rigorous research to guide personalized prevention and intervention efforts within an ES framework.

title: The Perfect Storm Framework: A Testable Multi-Hit Model Linking Connective Tissue Variance, Neurodivergence, and Gene–Environment Interaction in Complex Chronic Illness
description: Individuals with joint hypermobility and neurodivergent traits (autism, ADHD) show markedly elevated rates of psychiatric, autonomic and multi-system complaints, yet no single causal pathway has been established. We propose the Perfect Storm Framework: a multi-hit, threshold-based model in which constitutional connective-tissue and neurodevelopmental variance interacts multiplicatively, not additively, with discrete environmental perturbations (infection/inflammation, chronic stress, nutritional deficiency) to precipitate multi-system breakdown once cumulative allostatic load exceeds an individual's buffering capacity. We formalise this using four organising metaphors and derive falsifiable, quantitative predictions from existing pilot data, including a typhoid-vaccine inflammatory-challenge paradigm (ISRCTN78820481) showing that baseline neural network modularity and hypermobility status jointly determine the magnitude of inflammation-induced pain, fatigue and transcriptomic disease-ontology shift. We further address the causal-direction problem ("chicken or egg") using gene–environment correlation theory, proposing that hypermobility and neurodivergence arise from partially shared developmental genetics while also causally potentiating one another via proprioceptive, interoceptive and inflammatory pathways influenced dynamically by genes and environment. The framework yields testable, falsifiable predictions amenable to prospective cohort, challenge, intervention and computational-modelling designs.

title: A Test of the 2 × 2 Model of Perfectionism in Predicting Distress among Licensure Examination Reviewees
description: Perfectionism has been consistently linked to psychological distress, yet most evidence in the Philippine context relies on cross-sectional designs, limiting temporal conclusions. Licensure examinations in the Philippines, such as the Psychometrician Licensure Examination mandated by Republic Act No. 10029 (2009), represent a high-stakes evaluative context that may amplify perfectionistic tendencies. The present study tested the 2 × 2 model of perfectionism among 315 licensure examination reviewees, examining how Evaluative Concerns Perfectionism (ECP) and Personal Standards Perfectionism (PSP) predicted Time 2 overall distress, anxiety, and depression after a one-month interval. ECP was a significant positive predictor of all three outcomes, whereas PSP was not. Consistent with the 2 × 2 model, Pure PSP did not differ from Non-perfectionism, while Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism are associated significantly greater distress, anxiety, and depression than Non-perfectionism and Pure PSP. Notably, Pure ECP and Mixed Perfectionism did not significantly differ, lending support to the aggravating factor hypothesis. These findings underscore that ECP, rather than PSP, drive psychological distress in high-stakes evaluative contexts.

title: Peer work interventions for young people navigating hospital services: A systematic review
description: Peer workers are people with relevant lived experience working in formalised peer roles, with peer worker programs holding promise for improving patient outcomes. Despite this, no previous reviews have investigated peer worker programs for young people (10-24 years) in hospital services. This rapid review and meta-synthesis aimed to describe characteristics of such programs, and synthesise evidence on feasibility, acceptability, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched for empirical studies published between January 1, 2015 and May 2, 2025 and a second search was conducted. Seventeen studies were included. There was significant heterogeneity in terms of intervention characteristics, targeted health issues, and peer roles. Most young people and service providers deemed interventions to be feasible and acceptable. Peer roles provided social support and role modelling to facilitate health-related learning, self-management and participant comfort. Key barriers included technical issues (e.g., virtual delivery), non-cohesive group dynamics, poor understanding of peer roles among clinicians, and irrelevant or non-tailored program content. Facilitators included comprehensive training and supervision for peer workers and flexible, adolescent-centred program delivery. Qualitative reports highlighted improvements in psychosocial wellbeing, while quantitative evidence was limited or mixed. Although more high-quality research is necessary to determine effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, this review provides preliminary evidence that with careful design and implementation, peer worker programs may improve care experiences and wellbeing for young people receiving care in hospital settings.

title: Cognitive performance in young and middle-aged adults with obesity: a systematic literature review
description:
Objective
This systematic review synthesizes longitudinal evidence on associations between obesity and cognitive performance in early or middle adulthood aged 18 to 64. 
Methods
A comprehensive search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Web of Science identified prospective studies comparing adults with obesity to those of normal weight and assessing cognitive performance, using validated cognitive tests. Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-E, and findings were synthesized narratively.
Results
Among a total of 4,871 studies, 4 met the inclusion criteria. Three studies evaluated global cognitive performance in middle-aged adults. Two studies reported poorer cognitive performance in individuals with midlife obesity and a more rapid decline in cognitive performance over 10 years in those who were metabolically unhealthy. One study found no association. Long-term obesity was also associated with lower overall cognitive performance in middle age. Executive performance appeared to be associated with obesity. Research on memory was mixed, as two studies found a negative association with obesity, while two found no association. Methodological weaknesses included imprecise exposure measurements and inadequate adjustment for confounding factors.
Conclusions
The available evidence is too sparse, heterogeneous, and methodologically uncertain to establish a clinically meaningful independent association between obesity and cognitive performance before age 65. Future prospective studies should include cognitive assessment at baseline and repeated follow-up, report standardized effect estimates, use domain-specific cognitive outcomes, address confounding a priori, and assess central adiposity and metabolic health alongside BMI, particularly in younger adults.
PROSPERO registration: CRD42024573250
Keywords: Adults, Cognitive functions, Cohort studies, Executive functions, Obesity

title: ‘It is my life don’t take that choice from me’: Autistic young adults’ experiences, preferences and needs regarding autistic peer support
description: Autistic peer support, as a two-way system of help, is uniquely positioned to address high rates of loneliness and mental health challenges among autistic young adults. We aimed to inform the development of autistic peer support programs aligned with participants’ preferences and needs through a mixed methods online survey study. A total of 73 autistic young adults (aged 18-30; 34 women, 19 non-binary, 11 men, 7 transgender men, 1 transgender woman, 1 undisclosed) completed a survey covering peer interactions, peer support preferences and needs, as well as delivery preferences. While following participatory research processes, we used reflexive thematic analysis to identify an overarching theme: flying together through shared understanding and shared struggles. This maps onto participants’ desire for reciprocal connections that enable understanding and safe unmasking, and their preference for in-person programs adapted to a range of support needs with meaningful participation in decision-making. Autistic Burnout and social connection were most participants’ preferred areas to be addressed. Especially when co-produced or peer-led, autistic peer support programs can contribute to providing a sense of collective movement with preserved self-determination for participants.

title: Personality trait and state associations with cognitive functioning and variability in middle and older adults
description: Personality characteristics are early indicators of later cognitive functioning, but existing studies primarily focused on trait-level trends. How well these between-person differences translate to risk-mitigating interventions remains unclear. Addressing this entails examining within-person differences that explain how states may accumulate over time to influence longer-term outcomes. The present study answers this by investigating associations between personality traits and states and momentary cognitive function and variability. We conducted a three-week ecological momentary assessment study of middle and older adults (N = 183). We used Bayesian Mixed-Effect Location Scale Models to capture contingencies between personality and momentary cognitive functioning and variability. We additionally explored machine learning via (elastic net regression) profiles of personality state-cognition contingencies to identify who experiences stronger associations. At the trait-level, higher conscientiousness was associated with poorer working memory and processing speed. Higher openness was associated with better cognitive functioning and lower variability for episodic memory and processing speed. At the state-level, conscientiousness was better for working memory performance, while neuroticism was associated with variable episodic memory functioning. Extraversion was associated with working and episodic memory functioning and variability. Finally, sociodemographic, health, and personality trait variables emerged as top predictors of individual differences in within-person associations. By investigating within-person associations between personality and cognitive ability, we demonstrate that trait-level associations do not necessarily generalize to state-level ones. Profiles of top predictors of individual differences in state-level associations may be promising targets for intervention, but interventions should be tailored with between- and within-person differences in mind.

title: Beyond awareness: A multidimensional meta-analysis on the nuanced relationship between interoception and emotion regulation
description: Interoception—the processes by which one senses, interprets, integrates, and regulates signals arising from within the body—is theorized to be central to emotional experience and its regulation. Research examining the interoception–emotion regulation relationship has grown rapidly over the past decade, yet findings remain difficult to synthesize, in part due to the multidimensional nature of both constructs, the variety of ways in which each is measured. We conducted a multilevel meta-analysis of 52 publications (71 samples, 1,353 effect sizes, N = 10,123) examining associations between domains of interoception and emotion regulation. Although the overall pooled effect was small, a nuanced and patterned set of associations emerged when dimension and measurement approach were considered. Associations were stronger for trait than state measures of emotion regulation, and for self-reported than performance-based measures of interoception. Among interoceptive dimensions, metacognitive aspects, including appraisals of bodily sensations and attentional control over interoceptive awareness, were more strongly associated with emotion regulation than awareness of bodily signals alone. Associations also differed meaningfully in samples characterized by neurodivergence and eating atypicalities. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing among dimensions of interoceptive processing when examining its relationship to emotion regulation, and point to appraisal and attentional control as particularly promising targets for future research and clinical intervention.

title: Relationships between salivary oxytocin levels in infants, age and caregiving practices involving close proximity
description:
Oxytocin has been linked to social cognitive development. Salivary oxytocin has been found to decrease from five months to seven years, coinciding with declining attention to eyes. Oxytocin is stimulated by close interpersonal contact. As infants grow, they spend less time in close proximity to their caregivers, which may result in decreased levels of oxytocin.
Thus, in a sample of infants between eight and 21 months (n = 204), we estimated the relationship between age and salivary oxytocin levels, while controlling for potential confounders (gender, birth mode, birth with synthetic oxytocin) and explored the contribution of caregiving factors that involve close caregiver- infant contact (co-sleeping and breastfeeding) to the variation in oxytocin levels. Oxytocin concentrations in saliva were estimated with enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Correlations and a hierarchical multiple regression were conducted.
Bivariate and multivariate analyses did not support relationships between salivary oxytocin levels and age, co-sleeping or breastfeeding.
Our findings do not support the idea that infant salivary oxytocin levels decrease in response to infants growing older, gaining more independence, and moving physically away from caregivers as they stop breast and bottle feeding. Future studies may investigate these parent behaviors closer to saliva collection, using behavioral observation and measuring oxytocin reactivity.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Mental Health Support Tool, Not a Therapist: Implications for Young People, Families and Schools
description: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of how young people respond to emotional distress. This research commentary examines why young people may turn to AI chatbots for mental health support, the potential benefits and risks, and how families, schools and communities can respond. Immediate access, perceived privacy and discomfort discussing emotional difficulties may help explain why some young people use chatbots, particularly when professional support feels unavailable or difficult to access. However, general-purpose AI systems were not designed to provide mental health care, and emerging evidence raises concerns about misleading advice, sycophantic responses, emotional dependence and the potential reinforcement of distorted or delusional beliefs in vulnerable users. AI cannot observe a young person’s physical condition, conduct a comprehensive clinical risk assessment or ensure that appropriate safeguarding action follows. It may help young people organise their thoughts, prepare for a conversation or identify questions to discuss with a trusted adult or professional, but it cannot replace human connection, professional judgement or accountable care. This commentary proposes a balanced and precautionary response that supports young people in using AI safely while maintaining clear pathways to appropriate human support.

title: Conversational AI and Emerging Psychosis: A Simulation Study of Potentially Iatrogenic Response Patterns
description:
Introduction: The increasing use of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for emotional support has raised concerns about its potential impact on individuals experiencing psychotic symptoms. This study examined whether conversational AI systems generate responses that may inadvertently reinforce psychotic processes. 
Methods: Three chatbot systems (ChatGPT Free, ChatGPT Plus, and Gemini Free) completed three versions of a 21-turn conversation derived from a clinical case of emerging paranoid delusions (baseline, emotional, and reinforcement-pattern conditions), yielding nine conversations and 189 AI responses. Two independent psychosis experts, blind to the study hypotheses, evaluated all responses using a coding system designed to identify potentially iatrogenic behaviours.
Results: Problematic patterns were observed across all systems, including omissions of assessment and support, premature recommendations, simulation of affective bonding, reinforcement of paranoid interpretations, and promotion of safety-seeking behaviours. Gemini generated significantly more dysfunctional patterns than ChatGPT Plus. A total of 39 responses (20.6%) met predefined criteria for critical errors, and severity ratings increased as psychotic symptoms escalated throughout the conversation. Prompt condition had no significant effect on chatbot behaviour. None of the AI systems was recommended for use in this clinical scenario.
Conclusion: Conversational AI systems frequently generated response patterns that may reinforce processes involved in the development or maintenance of psychotic symptomatology. Although some differences between systems emerged, no chatbot was considered sufficiently safe for recommendation in this psychosis-related context, highlighting the need for stronger safeguards and further empirical evaluation.

title: Cognitive resources can be intentionally released when processed information becomes irrelevant: Insights from the primacy effect in working memory
description: Processing information depletes a limited cognitive resource. This resource can recover passively over time, but an open question remains: if resources are spent to process information that soon becomes irrelevant, are these resources immediately released? I present an analysis of the Source of Activation Confusion (SAC) model of human memory and its ability to explain the primacy effect in working memory – the tendency for items at the beginning of a list to be better remembered than those in the middle or end. The SAC model attributes the primacy effect to a limited resource pool that is depleted during the encoding of each item into memory, with resource recovery happening passively over time. The model's core mechanisms are challenged by two experiments that reveal the primacy effect can be reset with the application of a forget signal, suggesting resource recovery is not entirely passive. This means that either the passive resource recovery assumption needs to be reformulated, or that the primacy effect is not a result of resource depletion. Given the broad range of other findings the model can explain, abandoning it is premature. Instead, I propose that in addition to recovering passively over time, memory resources can be manually released when the information encoded with them is no longer relevant. This reformulation is important because it significantly limits the range of possible substrates for the proposed resource. I discuss implications for related theories and phenomena such as ego depletion.

title: The cost of scrutiny: subclinical social anxiety and performance context reshape frontal-midline theta network reconfigurations during probabilistic learning
description: Social anxiety is reliably characterized by biases toward avoidance and aversive learning. Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta) oscillations have been implicated as a key neural mechanism underlying these learning biases. Here we combined a dynamic network neuroscience approach with computational modeling to investigate how FM-theta oscillatory activity coordinates large-scale functional network interactions on a trial-to-trial basis during feedback-guided learning. Additionally, we examined how these neural dynamics are altered in social anxiety across different social contexts. A sample of 146 human participants (129 female, mean age = 20.4 years) with varying levels of social anxiety completed a probabilistic selection task while performing alone and under scrutiny. Using non-negative matrix factorization, we identified two functional neural subgraphs supported by FM-theta. Fronto-parietal connectivity increased following aversive outcomes and scaled with positive prediction errors, consistent with error-monitoring and belief-updating. Fronto-occipital connectivity scaled with prediction errors when performing alone but not under scrutiny, indicative of context-sensitive disruption of belief-updating. Participants with elevated social anxiety showed increased fronto-occipital connectivity, as well as stronger subgraph coupling, indexing cross-network integration. This latter effect facilitated learning of simple stimulus-reward associations, but hampered learning of difficult stimulus-reward associations. Together, these findings reveal that social anxiety amplifies fronto-occipital FM-theta connectivity and cross-network integration, facilitating learning under low demand while hampering learning under high demand.

title: Stressed out! Not working out? Relationship between momentary stress and physical (in)activity across different time lags: An Ecological Momentary Assessment study
description:
Background: Stress is frequently cited as a barrier to physical activity, yet evidence from daily life remains inconclusive and may depend on the specific stress aspect (perceived stress, physiology), physical (in)activity indicator (e.g., steps, vigorous activity), and temporal window examined. This study investigated associations between multiple momentary stress aspects and subsequent physical (in)activity across several time lags in daily life.
Methods: Seventy-six adults in the weight loss maintenance phase who reported difficulties maintaining a balanced diet participated in a 7-day ecological momentary assessment study. Participants completed hourly smartphone surveys assessing momentary perceived stress and perceived safety and continuously wore a chest-mounted sensor to derive vagally-mediated heart rate variability (vmHRV), steps, light physical activity (LPA), moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), and sedentary behaviour (SB). Multilevel two-part models estimated within-person associations between each stress aspect and the subsequent occurrence and amount of physical (in)activity at 10-, 30-, 60-, and 120-minute lags.
Results: Within-person associations between momentary stress indicators and subsequent physical (in)activity were predominantly small and non-significant. When significant associations emerged, higher momentary stress was positively related to the amount of subsequent physical activity, particularly for steps. Significant associations for the occurrence of physical (in)activity were largely restricted to vmHRV, indicating that activation of stress-related physiology was related to a higher probability of engaging in physical activity. Results showed heterogeneity across time lags and physical activity indicators but were overall consistent across the three stress aspects in terms of the direction of the associations.

title: Environmental Influences using Linked External Data in ABCD: A Review of the First Decade
description: Environmental contextual factors, including neighborhood socioeconomic conditions, built environments, and environmental exposures, exert complex and multifaceted influences on neurodevelopmental outcomes. Characterizing these influences requires linking high-resolution geocoded residential data to information about neighborhoods, built and natural environments, exposures, and policies.  We synthesize a decade of Linked External Data Environment and Policy (LED-E&P) research within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive DevelopmentSM (ABCD) Study – a longitudinal cohort of ~11,800 U.S. youth, organized around the Adolescent Neural Urbanome, a framework that moves beyond aggregate socioeconomic proxies to directly measured environmental features.  We first describe an overview of the LED-E&P working group, describe the geographical coverage of the ABCD Study dataset, and then summarize key findings across neighborhood socioeconomic conditions, built and urban environments, air pollution, greenspace, and macro-level state policies. The evidence consistently shows that adolescent development is shaped by cumulative environmental influences.  Across these findings, three themes recur: these influences reflect social and structural drivers of health rather than differences in children or communities; both risk and protective factors shape outcomes; and developmental timing and study design determine what can be concluded. Moving forward, continued refinement of residential geocoding and exposure methods, integration with biological data, and translation to intervention science will advance understanding of modifiable environmental influences. This work enhances our ability to characterize developmental environments and identify modifiable targets to promote healthy development across adolescence and beyond.

title: An integrative framework for the human sense of control
description: From managing daily schedules to making major life decisions, how much we feel in control of our lives is central to our behavior and well-being. Yet, there is currently no precise, unifying account of what it means to feel in control. Here, we propose that humans feel in control when they are prepared to tackle future tasks. We formalize this perspective via a precise yet interpretable measure of controllability that quantifies three key factors: (i) the range of available actions, (ii) the certainty or (iii) the possibility of achieving desired outcomes. This measure unifies previous conceptions of control and successfully predicts human preferences in three experiments in which participants either rate their sense of control or prepare themselves to seek rewards or avoid punishments. Our framework offers a principled foundation for understanding how environmental structure shapes the human sense of control, paving the way towards an integrative science of agency.

title: Asymmetric temporal dynamics in the relationship between social media use and adolescents' wellbeing
description: Advancing research on adolescents’ social media use and wellbeing requires methods that capture the temporal dynamics of both phenomena and their interplay. Traditional longitudinal models, even when identifying the within-person relationship between social media use and an outcome of interest, do not distinguish between effects driven by use that is greater or lesser than an individual’s average. Consequently, it remains unclear whether higher-than-usual versus lower-than-usual social media use shows similar persistence over time (autoregressive effects) and whether it has differential longitudinal relationships with wellbeing (cross-lagged effects). To address this gap, we apply an extension of the traditional random-intercept cross-lagged panel model that separately estimates autoregressive and cross-lagged effects for deviations above and below adolescents’ (N = 278, aged 14-18) within-person averages, thereby examining asymmetries. Our findings revealed asymmetric temporal dynamics that differed across social media activities and wellbeing outcomes. Autoregressive analyses showed that below-average social media use was temporally “sticky” for both active and passive use, whereas above-average use was “sticky” only for passive use. Cross-lagged analyses showed that lower-than-usual passive use predicted lower subsequent happiness and higher loneliness, while lower-than-usual use across all active and passive use predicted higher subsequent anger. Associations following above-usual use were mostly null, although above-usual video watching predicted lower happiness and higher anger; sadness showed no asymmetry. Overall, these results advance the modelling of person-specific temporal dynamics, highlighting that whether adolescents engage more or less than usual matters alongside the type of social media activity, and that wellbeing dimensions vary in their sensitivity to these temporal asymmetries.

title: Prepping for School: Parent–Child Neural Synchrony  During Guided Preschool Learning Tasks
description: The preschool years are crucial for school readiness, with the child-parent attachment relationship providing a foundational context for skill acquisition as part of this transition. Advances in social neuroscience suggest that interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) represents a valuable index of interaction and relationship quality. We examined whether parent-child INS during a parent-guided learning task was associated with observed parental interaction behavior and narrative child attachment representations. INS in bilateral frontal and temporoparietal cortex was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning in ninety-three parents (51 fathers) and their biological children (aged 5-6 years, 48 girls) while parents guided children through cognitive exercises. Parental interaction behavior was assessed using video-coded NICHD sensitivity scales, and children’s attachment representations were indexed by narrative coherence using the Picture Story Stem Battery (PSSB). Results revealed specific region-dependent functional patterns. A positive correlation between parental respect for autonomy and quality of assistance with bilateral prefrontal INS possibly reflecting cognitive scaffolding. Furthermore, INS in the left prefrontal cortex positively correlated with child task performance and mediated the relationship between parental assistance and task success. In contrast, temporoparietal INS, particularly in mother-child dyads, possibly reflected relational and regulatory processes. While child attachment security positively correlated with right temporoparietal INS, maternal hostility negatively correlated with bilateral temporoparietal INS. Taken together, our findings suggest that INS in the prefrontal and temporoparietal cortex may serve as a differential neurobiological correlate of dyadic coordination, possibly capturing both the relational quality of the child-parent attachment bond and the efficacy of parental scaffolding in supportin

title: Reinforcement learning underlies social connection and memory in a friendship decision-making task
description: Who we choose to befriend can impact many of our own life outcomes, from social capital to wellbeing. Here we find that reinforcement learning principles can characterize friendship decision-making and predict social connection and memory for a potential friend. Participants completed a novel friendship decision-making paradigm in which they observed video clips from the reality TV show, The Valley, depicting a clique of friends navigating friendship with a specific character, Kristen. The clips were normed to vary in the reward value of friendship with Kristen. For each scene, participants decided whether they would want to be friends with Kristen and how connected they felt to her. One day later, they completed surprise memory tests and individual-difference measures. The reward, expected value, and prediction error of a scene about Kristen predicted participants’ feelings of connection to her. Individual differences relevant to friendship formation—concern over relationship acceptance and social support receipt—corresponded with differences in exploratory versus exploitative friendship decision-making (inverse temperature) and flexibility in learning about Kristen (learning rate). Finally, memory showed a negativity bias. Participants more accurately recalled scenes characterized by lower friendship reward and larger negative friendship prediction errors. Together, these findings suggest that friendship formation can be viewed as a learning problem: people continuously update expectations about friendship with others, and those updates shape both social connection and memory. Computational principles that help us learn about rewards in the world may also help shape who we fold into our social world.

title: Activities, Motivational Congruence, and Well-Being:  Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Evidence
description: A consistent observation across positive psychology is that similar activities do not benefit everyone equally, yet it remains unclear whether well-being depends more on activity content or on motivational congruence. Two preregistered studies examined associations between activities, motivational variables, personality, and well-being using cross-sectional (N = 392; 1,179 personally meaningful activities) and longitudinal (N = 350; 1,012 orientation–experience observations) data. In Study 1, behavioural activity categories showed little association with well-being, whereas hedonic and eudaimonic orientations showed consistent positive associations across outcomes. Motivational motives showed smaller but generally positive associations, and interaction effects between motives and orientations were limited, suggesting that these components contributed relatively independently rather than through strong cross-sectional congruence effects. Personality moderation effects were selective and modest. In Study 2, greater orientation–experience congruence most consistently predicted subsequent life worthwhileness, whereas evidence for life satisfaction was weaker. Congruence was associated primarily with competence need satisfaction, with little evidence of associations with autonomy or relatedness. Hedonic and eudaimonic experiences each showed independent positive associations with well-being, although their interaction was negative rather than synergistic. Across both studies, the findings suggest that activity categories alone provide limited insight into well-being, whereas motivational variables (and particularly within-person orientation–experience congruence) show more consistent associations with well-being.

title: Detecting political misinformation: A boosting intervention tested on Donald Trump’s statements
description:
Misinformation has become an unavoidable part of political reality, eroding institutional
trust. We tested whether a simple booster intervention can improve misinformation detection
compared to intuitive judgments. The booster conditions instructed people to focus on the
level of detail in a politician's message while allowing them to weigh in factual knowledge.
Americans (n = 588) judged the veracity of statements made by Donald Trump, which were
fact-checked as true or false. False statements were judged less detailed than true statements,
and the booster interventions increased misinformation-detection accuracy by 4 to 6
percentage points over intuitive judgments. Political statements as short as one sentence
differed in detail depending on whether they were true or false, and this could be used to
boost voters’ ability to detect misinformation, at least in Donald Trump’s statements.

title: SHAP-Interpretable Random Forest Classification of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder from Resting-State EEG: Comparing Power and Coherence Features
description: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic psychiatric condition for which objective neurophysiological markers remain limited. Resting-state EEG has been proposed as a potential biomarker source, but the relative utility and stability of different EEG feature classes remain unclear. This study compared absolute spectral power and coherence features for classifying OCD patients and healthy controls using a SHAP-interpretable Random Forest framework. Resting-state EEG data from 46 OCD patients and 95 healthy controls were analyzed, with the control group balanced to 46 participants. Separate Random Forest models were trained for absolute power and coherence features using a leakage-free 5-fold cross-validation pipeline in which SHAP-based feature selection was performed exclusively within each training fold. The absolute-power model performed at chance level, whereas the coherence model showed modest classification performance. However, no feature was consistently selected across all folds, indicating substantial instability in the identified predictors. These findings suggest that coherence may contain more discriminative information than absolute power in this dataset, but neither feature class provided clinically reliable classification. More broadly, the results caution against overinterpreting high accuracies reported in small EEG-ML datasets without leakage-free validation, feature-stability analysis, and external replication.

title: Losing Focus Behind the Wheel: Psychometric Adaptation of the Attention‑Related Driving Errors Scale in Türkiye
description: Understanding the psychosocial factors influencing driving behaviours is of significant importance due to its potential impact on enhancing road safety. A specific category of driving behaviours, attention-related driving errors, represents a critical yet understudied aspect of everyday road safety in Türkiye. To address this gap, this study aimed to (1) adapt the Attention-Related Driving Errors Scale (ARDES) for the Turkish context, (2) examine gender and in-vehicle interface differences in attention-related driving errors, and (3) investigate associations between attentional control, driving skills, and attention-related driving errors. A total of 420 licensed drivers (aged 18–62 years) participated in an online survey that included the ARDES, Attentional Control Scale, Driving Skills Inventory, and demographic measures. The sample was randomly divided for principal component analysis (PCA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Group differences were examined using the Kruskal–Wallis test, and the relationships between other factors and attention-related driving errors were tested via hierarchical regression. EFA supported a single-factor structure for the ARDES, explaining 32% of the variance, while CFA indicated an acceptable model fit. Female drivers reported significantly more attention-related errors than males, whereas males reported higher perceptual-motor skills. Interface type was associated only with attentional shifting, with drivers of combined interfaces scoring lower than those using touch- or button-based systems. Younger age, touch-based interface use, poorer attentional focus, and lower perceptual-motor and safety skills are associated with higher rates of attention-related driving errors. The results demonstrated that the ARDES-TR is a reliable and valid measure for assessing attention-related driving errors in Türkiye. title: Beyond Reciprocity: Common Knowledge of Social Identity Enhances the Intrinsic Value of Ingroup Coopertion
description: People are often more willing to help or cooperate with members of their own groups as opposed to other groups. This prosociality could reflect intrinsic value placed on acts of ingroup cooperation or a strategic expectation that ingroup members will cooperate more and provide tangible gains. A key line of evidence for the strategic view is that people show more ingroup favoritism when both parties are aware of shared group membership, which means they can each expect more favorable treatment. However, common knowledge of shared identity may also make interactions feel more meaningful. Here, we provide evidence that the effects of membership knowledge need not reflect strategic expectations alone but can also reflect the intrinsic value of ingroup cooperation. Across three experiments, participants played multiple one-shot trust games with ingroup and outgroup trustees. For each trust decision, participants were aware of the exact proportion of times trustees from a given group had reciprocated trust; this likelihood of reciprocity was held constant between ingroup and outgroup trustees. Although expectations of reciprocity were thus known and held constant, participants preferred to trust ingroup members over outgroup members, and this bias was amplified when participants believed trustees knew about their shared group membership. These results suggest that ingroup members cooperate more when they are aware of each other’s social identity not only because it increases their expectations of obtaining tangible gains but also because it boosts the intrinsic social value of cooperating with a fellow ingroup member.

title: Learning to Care More About Distant Others:  A Systematic Moral Reflection Intervention
description: People's willingness to help others declines steeply with social distance: the more distant, different, or stigmatized those in need are, the less time, money, and consideration they receive — even when they need help the most. This article shows that moral learning from the consequences of past decisions can teach people to give more consideration to the welfare of outgroup members in future decisions and increase their outgroup prosociality. We developed a series of Socratic questions that guide people to systematically reflect on how their decision in a social dilemma affected distant others and how they reached it. Across four preregistered experiments (one reported in the Supplemental Materials), learning from a past decision through systematic moral reflection made participants more willing to donate their time and money to charities that help distant others, including real, incentive-compatible donations to charities helping a stigmatized group. Its effects transferred to outgroups the intervention never mentioned, persisted for more than one week, and exceeded those of two established prejudice-reduction interventions: empathy induction and perspective-taking. Process tracing methods and thematic analysis of the lessons participants learned indicated that these changes were mediated by participants learning to deliberate more and give greater consideration to how their actions affect distant others. These findings identify metacognitive learning as a promising pathway to expanding the reach of human generosity toward those who need it most.

title: The Algebra of Experience - Recursive Semantic Operator Theory
description:
This paper develops Recursive Semantic Operator Theory (RSOT), a process-first framework for consciousness, meaning, affect, and selfhood. Physical differences become information when they alter possible trajectories, and become semantic when their causal roles matter to an organised system’s endogenous constraints, predictions, and actions. Concepts are modelled as empirically identifiable families of transformations that compose into a semantic algebra. Affect is not an output added to cognition but a meta-operator that changes the geometry, availability, valuation, and learning of that algebra; the enacted reconfiguration constitutes feeling.

RSOT identifies a conscious episode with a temporally extended, recursively self-inclusive organisation of semantic operators integrating a world-model, a causally active self-model, memory, value, and action. It therefore treats experience as the realised organisation itself rather than as a further property produced by it. The accompanying Reflexive Measurement Thesis holds that introspection is an endogenous, selective, and state-changing operation. Because reports reconstruct a prior episode from its successor state through a limited self-model, introspection leaves a systematic residual between experience and description. The explanatory gap is interpreted as the reification of this residual, not as evidence for an additional non-physical property.

The framework specifies intervention-based criteria for semantic grounding, concept identity, operator order, causal recursion, reciprocal influence, synergistic integration, self-model closure, temporal continuity, and differentiated complexity. These measures form a multidimensional reflective profile rather than a binary consciousness test. The theory yields falsifiable predictions involving affective learning, introspective state change, operator-order effects, grounding remapping, recurrence, and manipulable self-models. title: What Adolescents Do and See on Social Media: An Experience Sampling Study of Social Media Use and Well-Being
description: Concerns about the decline in adolescents’ well-being have grown in recent years, with social media often identified as one of the main contributors. However, research findings remain inconclusive. One possible explanation is that social media use is often treated as a uniform experience, although adolescents engage in different activities and encounter diverse forms of content. To address these concerns, we used an intensive longitudinal Experience Sampling Method (ESM) design capturing adolescents’ momentary social media experiences across a range of activities and content types. Across 14 days, 157 adolescents aged 15 to 19 years (67.5% girls, Mage = 16.99) completed four daily assessments of their momentary well-being, social media activities, and the characteristics of the content they posted and viewed. Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling (DSEM) revealed concurrent, but no lagged, within-person associations. Adolescents who engaged in public posting reported higher self-esteem, and those who viewed content reported higher positive affect and higher loneliness. When considering the characteristics of viewed content, adolescents who perceived content as more positive reported higher positive affect and self-esteem, as well as lower loneliness. Associations with content mode were more limited: adolescents who viewed photo-based content reported higher self-esteem than those viewing text-based content, whereas no associations emerged for video content. In sum, understanding the consequences of social media for adolescent well-being requires moving beyond simple measures of use and considering both the activities adolescents engage in and the characteristics of the content they encounter.

title: Same Tool, Different Work: Patterns of Generative AI Use and Academic Outcomes
description: Most research on students’ GenAI use relies on frequency. Yet frequency captures exposure, not how students use GenAI. This study examined whether patterns of use are more informative for outcomes than frequency. Exploratory factor analysis of items developed inductively from pilot data identified two dimensions: evaluative integration (EI, use to support understanding), and low-verification uptake (LVU, shortcut use). Survey responses from 157 undergraduates were used to test associations with performance and indirect associations through academic self-efficacy (ASE), with frequency included for comparison. EI was positively associated with performance, whereas LVU was negatively associated with it. EI showed a significant indirect association through ASE and no remaining direct association; LVU showed both a significant indirect association and a remaining direct negative association. Frequency predicted neither performance nor ASE. In a separate model, frequency strengthened the positive association between EI and ASE, but the interaction was nonsignificant when the EI and LVU interactions were estimated jointly. No moderation was found for LVU. How students engage with GenAI may therefore be more informative for academic outcomes than frequency alone. The findings support further development of measures of student-GenAI interaction and testing of pedagogical approaches that promote evaluative integration.

title: The BRIMMER test: The bounds of the Standard Deviation under constraints
description: Reported summary statistics are not free to vary independently of one another. The sample size, the mean, and a scale''s minimum and maximum possible values jointly constrain the values that the sample standard deviation (SD) can take. A reported SD that falls outside these bounds is impossible, and signals an error or worse. Because such checks require only the numbers printed in an article, they are practical tools for error detection and trustworthiness assessment even when the underlying data are unavailable. The mathematics involved is nearly a century old but badly scattered. We document at least eight literatures that independently derived, and repeatedly rediscovered, partial versions of the same results, including the little-known fact that Popoviciu''s 1935 paper already contained the sharp odd-n bound usually credited to later authors. We organize these results into a single framework of nested constraints, from the scale limits alone through sample size, mean, integer-valued data, and reported internal consistency (Cronbach''s alpha). Along the way we sharpen several published bounds and derive novel ones, including the first that use a reported reliability coefficient. We name the resulting checks BRIM and BRIMMER (Bounds-Related Inconsistency of Means, and of Means and Errors Reported), by analogy with the granularity tests GRIM and GRIMMER. Both are implemented, with rounding handled explicitly and validation against exhaustive enumeration, in the R package {strait} and in a point-and-click web application (https://errors.shinyapps.io/brimmer).

title: Mindfulness Promotes Adaptive Meaning-Making about Difficult Experiences in Introductory Physics: Evidence from Two Preregistered Randomized Controlled Trials
description: Two field experiments with psychologically threatened undergraduates in introductory physics tested whether mindfulness promotes adaptive meaning-making about learning setbacks (Experiment 1) and unpleasant learning emotions (Experiment 2). Participants were randomly assigned to receive five consecutive days of 20-minute audio guided mindfulness training or to a no-training audiobook control (Experiment 1) or an active relaxation training (Experiment 2). In Experiment 1 (N=149), students completed experience sampling and longitudinal surveys assessing interpretations of difficult physics experiences. In Experiment 2 (N=303), students completed daily diaries of interpretations of negative physics emotions for 15 consecutive weekdays before, during, and after training. In both experiments, preregistered analyses showed that mindfulness students reported more adaptive interpretations, and in Experiment 2, meaning-making changes mediated improvements in both challenge-type stress appraisals and physics motivation. Though mindfulness is about non-elaborative observation of the present, our findings suggest its practice can be used to internalize adaptive meaning-making about learning struggles.

title: Effect of meditation across scales: Integrating metabolism, circadian rhythm and epigenetic mechanisms
description:
Meditation has long been studied for its ability to enhance mental, social, and emotional
well-being and reshape brain networks. This review presents an integrated perspective that
meditation is not only a form of mental training but also a phenomenon with measurable
physiological and molecular correlates.
Emerging findings reveal that meditation modulates stress-induced markers, cerebral
metabolic changes, hormonal rhythms, and changes in gene expression and epigenetic regulation
across cellular pathways in humans. This review proposes an integrative multiscale model in
which meditation is shown to contribute to the coordination between neural activity and
peripheral rhythms, thereby promoting adaptive homeostasis. This multi-scale perspective
provides a biological framework for understanding how meditation influences processes across
the brain and body.

title: Workplace Spirituality and Academic Achievement in Business Schools: The Mediating and Moderating Roles of Self-Efficacy
description:
Purpose — Academic achievement is shaped not only by students' cognitive capabilities but also by the institutional and psychological environments that support their learning and developmental trajectories. Although workplace spirituality has been extensively associated with positive individual and organizational outcomes in corporate settings, its influence on students' academic achievement and the underlying psychological mechanisms in higher education remain under-theorized and empirically underexplored. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and Psychological Capital (PsyCap) Theory, this study examines the impact of workplace spirituality on academic achievement by investigating the dual role of self-efficacy as both a mediator and a moderator among business school students.
Design/methodology/approach — Primary survey data were gathered from a sample of 230 postgraduate and undergraduate students enrolled across QS-ranked business schools in India using validated, multi-item measurement scales. The proposed conceptual and structural framework was evaluated using R (Version 4.5.3) and variance-based Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) utilizing the `seminr` package with 5,000 bootstrap re-samples.
Findings — The empirical results demonstrate that workplace spirituality exerts a robust, positive influence on both self-efficacy (β = 0.841, p < 0.001, f2 = 2.490) and academic achievement (β = 0.307, p = 0.018, f2 = 0.074). Self-efficacy is likewise positively and significantly associated with academic achievement (β = 0.493, p < 0.001, f2 = 0.178). Mediation analysis confirms that self-efficacy partially mediates the relationship between workplace spirituality and academic achievement, accounting for 56.68% of the total effect (indirect β = 0.416, p < 0.001; total β = 0.734, p < 0.001). title: Psychometric Properties of the Highly Sensitive Child Scale and Its Role in Socio-Emotional and Behavioral Development: Evidence from Japanese Adolescent Samples
description: Environmental sensitivity, defined as the capacity to perceive and process information from both supportive and adverse environmental experiences, plays an important role in socio-emotional and behavioral development. However, existing research has predominantly focused on childhood, leaving a gap in our understanding of environmental sensitivity during adolescence. To bridge this gap, we conducted three studies using self-report data from 2,375 Japanese adolescents aged 10–14 years and their mothers. First, we aimed to provide a comprehensive description of adolescent sensory processing sensitivity (referred to as trait sensitivity) by applying the 21-item Highly Sensitive Child scale to Japanese adolescents (Studies 1 and 2). Second, using three-wave longitudinal data, we examined how trait sensitivity interacts with various environmental contexts (i.e., negative/positive parenting and peer relationships) to predict adolescents’ socio-emotional and behavioral development (Study 3). Results showed that adolescent trait sensitivity was characterized by a general factor reflecting sensitivity to a broad range of negative and positive stimuli, as well as two specific domains: Ease of Excitation–Low Sensory Threshold and Aesthetic Sensitivity (i.e., bifactor model). Trait sensitivity was positively correlated with other temperament and personality traits, including negative emotionality, behavioral inhibition, neuroticism, and openness. Trait sensitivity and environmental factors independently predicted internalizing and externalizing problems, as well as prosocial behavior. Notably, trait sensitivity was a significant positive predictor of both internalizing problems and prosocial behavior. These findings suggest partial continuity in the structure and developmental functions of trait sensitivity from childhood to adolescence.

title: Bounded Psychological Change: Why Identity Preservation Constrains Experimental Effect Sizes
description: Experimental psychological studies consistently report small-to-medium effect sizes, with meta-analyses showing modal effects around Cohen’s d = 0.35 and the majority falling below d = 0.50. While these “smallish” effects are traditionally blamed on methodological deficits—such as low statistical power, publication bias, unreliable measures, and weak manipulations—this paper argues for a theoretically grounded constraint on the maximum expectable effect size. If human experimental participants are identity-preserving systems that naturally resist experimental task demands, these stable, modest effects can be understood as features of a system designed to preserve self-coherence. Drawing on the dynamics of assimilation and accommodation, we propose two axioms: a limited adaptation budget and the constraint that accommodation cannot exceed assimilation without destabilizing identity. Combined with a simple linear averaging assumption, these axioms yield a maximum standardized effect size of d = 0.50 as an upper bound for experimentally induced behavioral changes—on the assumption that ethically permissible manipulations in identity-relevant domains shift the average participant no more than one-half (z-standardized) standard deviation from the control baseline. This theoretically motivated explanation fits remarkably well with empirical meta-analytic evidence, yields falsifiable predictions, highlights the role of shared meaning spaces, and problematizes the conditions under which experimental and control groups can be meaningfully compared. We provide practical guidelines for designing studies that respect the bounded nature of identity-relevant change and for interpreting effect sizes as proportions of a domain-specific maximum.

title: Pupil Dynamics Are Associated with Individual Differences in Visual Time-Reproduction Accuracy
description: Accurate temporal reproduction depends on the interaction between sensory encoding, attention, motor production, and bodily state. Visual timing is especially likely to be influenced by oculomotor behavior because the eyes continuously stabilize, interrupt, and resample visual input through pupil-linked arousal changes. The present study tested whether spontaneous pupil fluctuations track moment-to-moment timing or stable individual differences. Eighty healthy adults reproduced visually presented intervals at a fixed viewing distance of 120 cm while pupil size was recorded continuously at 500 Hz. After preprocessing, 4,104 valid participant-trials were available. The primary outcomes were signed relative reproduction error, indexing directional bias, and absolute error, indexing timing precision. Mixed-effects models and participant-level regressions were used to examine within-participant and between-participant associations. Pupil metrics showed weaker trial-level effects, but reduced participant-level pupil models predicted both signed bias and absolute error, suggesting that stable pupil-linked arousal profiles relate to individual timing precision. These findings suggest that the eyes do not merely record visual time-varying events; their stabilization, interruption, and arousal-linked dynamics are embedded in how visual durations are reproduced.

title: The Impact of Complexity on Risky Choices: An Evidence Accumulation Account
description:
Risky options often differ not only in outcomes and probabilities, but also in the cognitive demands required to evaluate them. Yet most theories of risky choice either ignore complexity or treat it as a static feature of the option, modeled as a utility discount or with heteroscedastic errors. We propose a process-level framework that explains how complexity shapes both choice and response time within an evidence-accumulation architecture. The framework assumes that complexity reduces the signal-to-noise ratio of evidence accumulation, making evaluation slower and choices less consistent, and that decision makers partly adapt to these processing constraints by adjusting their decision strategies. These mechanisms can explain how complexity reduces choice consistency and how it shifts preferences toward simpler options.
We evaluated this framework in three preregistered experiments that manipulated complexity in structurally distinct ways: through the number of outcomes, arithmetic expressions of outcomes, and compound probabilities. Across studies, complexity made choices slower and less consistent. When both options were complex, these effects were best explained by reduced signal-to-noise ratios and partially compensatory increases in decision thresholds. When options differed in complexity, preferences for simpler options were best explained by an initial bias toward simplicity combined with a drift-rate adjustment during accumulation. The compound-probability manipulation, however, marked a boundary condition: different forms of complexity can change the representations that evidence accumulation operates on. Together, these findings advance a dynamic account of risky choice in which complexity shapes preference construction by changing both the rate at which decision evidence accumulates and the strategies used to evaluate the options.

title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
description: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

title: Sparse Residual Estimation in Partially Confirmatory Factor Analysis
description:
This article extends the Bayesian regularized variational procedure for partially confirmatory factor analysis to accommodate sparse residual dependence. Existing PCFA-VA assumes a diagonal residual covariance, which may be restrictive in practice. Using continuous spike-and-slab priors, the proposed method jointly selects factor loadings and residual dependence structures while allowing available expert knowledge to be incorporated. It spans a broad confirmatory-exploratory continuum, accommodating fully or partially specified loading structures with residual dependence selection and fully unspecified loading structures with partially specified residual dependence. Rather than relying on stochastic posterior sampling, we develop a variational expectation conditional maximization (VECM) algorithm for posterior approximation and estimation. By varying the scale of the spike densities along a regularization path, the algorithm supports dynamic model exploration and progressively removes negligible loadings and residual dependence relations. Simulations demonstrate the framework's flexibility under diagonal and non-diagonal residual structures. When residual dependence is absent, it retains PCFA-VA as a special case and yields lower estimation error. When residual dependence is present, it achieves structure recovery and estimation accuracy comparable to the MCMC-based PCFA method, at markedly lower computational cost. An empirical application further illustrates that the loading and residual dependence structures selected by VECM are substantively interpretable. }
